citations.quote:
If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

derivations.claim: In positive dimension, if $M_ex=0$, then $x^TM_ex=0$, so positive definiteness gives $x=0$; the same argument applies to $M_b$. In dimension zero the unique square matrix is the identity map on the singleton space and is invertible. Thus both matrices are injective and hence invertible in their finite-dimensional domains, so their inverse operations used by consumers are defined in every allowed dimension.

For $u\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$ and $v\in\ker C$, $\langle C^Tu,v\rangle=u^TCv=0$, hence $\operatorname{im}C^T\subseteq(\ker C)^\perp$. Also $z\in(\operatorname{im}C^T)^\perp$ exactly when $u^TCz=0$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$, which is exactly $Cz=0$; therefore $(\operatorname{im}C^T)^\perp=\ker C$. By [F1], decompose any $w\in(\ker C)^\perp$ as $w=u+v$ with $u\in\operatorname{im}C^T$ and $v\in(\operatorname{im}C^T)^\perp=\ker C$. Both $w$ and $u$ are orthogonal to $v$, so $\lVert v\rVert^2=\langle w-u,v\rangle=0$ and $v=0$. Hence $(\ker C)^\perp=\operatorname{im}C^T$.
Assume $\operatorname{im}G=\ker C$. If $q=0$, then $G^TM_ee=0$, so $M_ee$ is orthogonal to every column of $G$ and hence to $\ker C$. By step 1.2, $M_ee\in\operatorname{im}C^T$.

Conversely, if $M_ee\in\operatorname{im}C^T$, then step 1.2 gives $M_ee\in(\ker C)^\perp$. Every column of $G$ lies in $\ker C$, so $G^TM_ee=0$ and therefore $q=0$. The two implications prove the stated characterization.

boundaries.evidence: The definition permits n_e=n_b=0; the unique empty mass matrices are identities, positive definiteness is vacuous, and step 1.1 proves invertibility while step 1.2 covers the zero spaces.
Step 2.1 includes the zero state in the conditional characterization, and the displayed definitions give W=0 and q=0 there.
The one-dimensional case is included in steps 1.1–3.1; all kernel and orthogonal-complement arguments remain valid.
The allowed n_g=0 case and C=0 case are covered by steps 1.2–3.1, including the empty-column basis for a zero kernel.

boundaries.reason: The system is defined on an open time interval and makes no endpoint regularity assertion.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 uses only the finite-dimensional orthogonal decomposition supplier; no arbitrary-index choice is used.
Step 2.1 proves q=0 implies M_e e belongs to im C^T when im G=ker C.
Step 3.1 proves M_e e in im C^T implies q=0 when im G=ker C.

Let $n_e,n_b,n_c,n_g$ be nonnegative integers. For dimension zero, $\mathbb R^0$ has its single empty vector and its unique square matrix acts as the identity on that space. Choose real matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$ and $M_b\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_b}$ that are symmetric positive definite, meaning $M_e^T=M_e$, $M_b^T=M_b$, $x^TM_ex>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and $y^TM_by>0$ for every nonzero $y\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$; these positivity conditions are vacuous on $\mathbb R^0$. Choose $C\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_e}$, a symmetric positive semidefinite $S\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$, meaning $S^T=S$ and $x^TSx\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and matrices $D\in\mathbb R^{n_c\times n_b}$ and $G\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_g}$ satisfying $DC=0$ and $CG=0$. These are finite real matrix data; no mesh or continuum field is assumed.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $j:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ be continuous, and let candidate states $e:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ and $b:I\to\mathbb R^{n_b}$ be of class $C^1$. The **finite compatible matrix system** is

$$M_e\dot e(t)=C^TM_bb(t)-Se(t)-j(t),\qquad \dot b(t)=-Ce(t)\quad(t\in I).$$

Its quadratic **energy** is $W(e,b):=\tfrac12(e^TM_ee+b^TM_bb)$. Its magnetic constraint is the vector $Db\in\mathbb R^{n_c}$. For the chosen $G$, its weak-divergence coordinate is $q:=-G^TM_ee\in\mathbb R^{n_g}$. The term “weak-divergence” names this finite-dimensional quantity only. If the columns of $G$ form a basis of $\ker C:=\{v\in\mathbb R^{n_e}:Cv=0\}$, then $q=0$ exactly when $M_ee\in\operatorname{im}C^T:=\{C^Tu:u\in\mathbb R^{n_b}\}$.

For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

For bounded $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, in the metric sense of [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], its **Jordan outer content** is the infimum of $\sum_{r<q}\operatorname{vol}(R_r)$ over finite axis-parallel rectangle covers of $E$. Its **Jordan inner content** is the supremum of the same sums over finite families of rectangles contained in $E$ whose interiors are pairwise disjoint.

Metric boundedness always supplies a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. For
nonempty $E$, choose $x_0\in\mathbb R^m$ and $r>0$ with
$E\subseteq B(x_0,r)$. Since
$|x_j-(x_0)_j|\le d_\infty(x,x_0)\le d_2(x,x_0)<r$ for every coordinate
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] clause 3, [[def-metric-ball]]), the nondegenerate box
$\prod_{j<m}[(x_0)_j-r,(x_0)_j+r]$ contains $E$. The empty set lies in
any fixed nondegenerate rectangle.

Thus the outer family is nonempty and the same bounding rectangle bounds the
inner sums; the empty family gives inner sum $0$. Refining all listed
endpoints into one grid and splitting the nested finite sums shows every
inscribed sum is at most every covering sum
([[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).
Completeness therefore supplies finite real extrema
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]],
[[lem-sup-unique]]).

The set is **Jordan measurable** when the contents agree, and their common value is its **Jordan content**. The empty set and every degenerate rectangle have content $0$.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
(Interior, closure, boundary and exterior of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

A **grid partition** $P$ of a nondegenerate rectangle $Q=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a family, one for each $j<m$, of one-dimensional partitions $a_j=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,n_j}=b_j$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]). For a multi-index $i=(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ with $i_j<n_j$, its cell is
$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$
These statements include boundary overlaps: boundaries may meet, but interiors do not, and volume splitting is algebraic.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

derivations.claim: Put $z=(e,b)\in\mathbb R^{n_e+n_b}$ and define $A:=\begin{pmatrix}-M_e^{-1}S&M_e^{-1}C^TM_b\\-C&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $f(t):=\begin{pmatrix}-M_e^{-1}j(t)\\0\end{pmatrix}$. The inverses exist by positive definiteness in [F1]: if $M_ex=0$, then $x^TM_ex=0$ forces $x=0$, and an injective square map in finite dimensions is invertible; the same holds for $M_b$. Thus the system is exactly $z'=Az+f(t)$.

Let $g(s):=e^{-(s-t_0)A}f(s)$ and $H(t):=\int_{t_0}^t g(s)\,ds$, interpreting each coordinate as a Riemann integral and using the oriented convention $\int_a^b=-\int_b^a$ when $b<a$ and $\int_a^a=0$. If $n_e+n_b=0$, then $g(s)$ and $H(t)$ are the unique empty vector for all $s,t$, so $H'=g$ vacuously. Otherwise, on every nondegenerate compact segment in $I$, each coordinate of $g$ is continuous, so [F3] gives integrability and [F4] defines $H$. For each coordinate $k$, the cut-additivity in [F6], together with the oriented convention, gives $H_k(t+h)-H_k(t)=\int_t^{t+h}g_k(s)\,ds$ whenever $t,t+h\in I$: positive-oriented additivity follows by splitting at an interior point, and reversing endpoints or using a zero-length interval gives the other endpoint orders. Thus, for $h\ne0$, $\frac{H_k(t+h)-H_k(t)}{h}-g_k(t)=\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}(g_k(s)-g_k(t))\,ds$, where [F7] evaluates the integral of the constant $g_k(t)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, continuity of $g_k$ at $t$ gives $\delta>0$ such that $|g_k(s)-g_k(t)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $|s-t|<\delta$; since $I$ is open, reduce $\delta$ so $[t-\delta,t+\delta]\subset I$. If $0<|h|<\delta$, then on $J=[\min(t,t+h),\max(t,t+h)]$ the absolute-value estimate and monotonicity in [F6], followed by [F7], give $\left|\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}(g_k(s)-g_k(t))\,ds\right|\le\frac1{|h|}\int_J|g_k(s)-g_k(t)|\,ds\le\varepsilon$. Therefore each coordinate has derivative $g_k(t)$ and $H'(t)=g(t)$ throughout $I$.

Define $z(t):=e^{(t-t_0)A}(z_0+H(t))$, where $z_0=(e_0,b_0)$. By [F2] and step 1.2, the product rule gives $z'=Az+f(t)$, since $e^{(t-t_0)A}e^{-(t-t_0)A}=I$ by the commuting-product identity in [F2]; also $z(t_0)=z_0$. Thus a $C^1$ solution exists on all of $I$. If $n_e+n_b=0$, every state is the unique empty vector, so the solution is unique. Otherwise, if $\widetilde z$ is another solution with the same initial value, then $\xi(t):=e^{-(t-t_0)A}(\widetilde z(t)-z(t))$ has derivative zero by [F2] and the two differential equations. Each coordinate of $\xi$ is constant by [F5] and vanishes at $t_0$, so $\widetilde z=z$.

Differentiate $W=\tfrac12(e^TM_ee+b^TM_bb)$ and substitute the system equations. Symmetry of $M_e,M_b$ gives $\dot W=e^T(C^TM_bb-Se-j)+b^TM_b(-Ce)=-e^TSe-e^Tj$, because the real scalar cross terms $e^TC^TM_bb$ and $b^TM_bCe$ are equal and cancel.
The magnetic quantity satisfies $(Db)'=D\dot b=-DCe=0$ by [F1]; each coordinate is constant by [F5], and its value at $t_0$ is $Db(t_0)$.
Since $q=-G^TM_ee$, differentiation and the first system equation give $\dot q=-G^T(C^TM_bb-Se-j)=-(CG)^TM_bb+G^T(Se+j)=G^T(Se+j)$, using $CG=0$ from [F1]. This proves all three identities.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
The operator norm is zero on the zero domain and otherwise is max_{||v||=1} ||Tv|| is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $n_e,n_b,n_c,n_g$ be nonnegative integers. For dimension zero, $\mathbb R^0$ has its single empty vector and its unique square matrix acts as the identity on that space. Choose real matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$ and $M_b\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_b}$ that are symmetric positive definite, meaning $M_e^T=M_e$, $M_b^T=M_b$, $x^TM_ex>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and $y^TM_by>0$ for every nonzero $y\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$; these positivity conditions are vacuous on $\mathbb R^0$. Choose $C\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_e}$, a symmetric positive semidefinite $S\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$, meaning $S^T=S$ and $x^TSx\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and matrices $D\in\mathbb R^{n_c\times n_b}$ and $G\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_g}$ satisfying $DC=0$ and $CG=0$. These are finite real matrix data; no mesh or continuum field is assumed.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $j:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ be continuous, and let candidate states $e:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ and $b:I\to\mathbb R^{n_b}$ be of class $C^1$. The **finite compatible matrix system** is

$$M_e\dot e(t)=C^TM_bb(t)-Se(t)-j(t),\qquad \dot b(t)=-Ce(t)\quad(t\in I).$$

Its quadratic **energy** is $W(e,b):=\tfrac12(e^TM_ee+b^TM_bb)$. Its magnetic constraint is the vector $Db\in\mathbb R^{n_c}$. For the chosen $G$, its weak-divergence coordinate is $q:=-G^TM_ee\in\mathbb R^{n_g}$. The term “weak-divergence” names this finite-dimensional quantity only. If the columns of $G$ form a basis of $\ker C:=\{v\in\mathbb R^{n_e}:Cv=0\}$, then $q=0$ exactly when $M_ee\in\operatorname{im}C^T:=\{C^Tu:u\in\mathbb R^{n_b}\}$.

Inputs are real matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$ and $M_b\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_b}$ that are symmetric positive definite, $C\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_e}$, and compatible matrices $D,G$ satisfying $DC=CG=0$, with $S=0$ and $j\equiv0$ in the finite compatible matrix system. All dimensions are nonnegative integers as in that system. Also input a real step size $h>0$, an integer horizon $N\ge0$, and initial vectors $e_0\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$ and $b_{-1/2}\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$. The matrix $M_e$ is positive definite, so each mass equation below has a unique exact solution, including the unique empty solve when $n_e=0$. For each integer $n=0,1,\ldots,N-1$, first set

$$b_{n+1/2}:=b_{n-1/2}-hCe_n,$$

then solve uniquely for $v_n\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$ in

$$M_ev_n=C^TM_bb_{n+1/2}$$

and set $e_{n+1}:=e_n+h v_n$. Output the electric vectors $e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ and magnetic vectors $b_{-1/2},b_{1/2},\ldots,b_{N-1/2}$. When $N=0$, the loop makes no updates and the output consists only of the two initial vectors. Every mass solve is exact; no inexact-solve error model is part of this procedure.

derivations.claim: For a zero-dimensional mass space, the unique square matrix is the identity, its own inverse, and its root. In positive dimension, $M_e$ and $M_b$ are symmetric and therefore self-adjoint in the standard Euclidean inner product; by [F1] each has an orthonormal eigenbasis. If $v$ is a unit eigenvector of either matrix with eigenvalue $\lambda$, positive definiteness in [F6] gives $\lambda=v^TMv>0$. Define the square root to act by $\sqrt\lambda$ on the full $\lambda$-eigenspace, and its inverse to act by $1/\sqrt\lambda$ there. These definitions are independent of a basis choice within an eigenspace, satisfy $(M^{1/2})^2=M$ and $M^{-1/2}M^{1/2}=I$, and agree with the Statement's root convention.

Let $x_n=M_e^{1/2}e_n$ and $y_{n-1/2}=M_b^{1/2}b_{n-1/2}$. Multiplying the first update in [F7] by $M_b^{1/2}$ gives $y_{n+1/2}=y_{n-1/2}-hKx_n$. Multiplying the second update by $M_e^{1/2}$ and using the root identities from step 1.1 gives $x_{n+1}=x_n+hK^Ty_{n+1/2}$.

Write $x=x_n$, $y=y_{n-1/2}$, $y'=y_{n+1/2}$, and $x'=x_{n+1}$. From step 2.1, $x'=x+hK^Ty'$ and $y'=y-hKx$. Expanding gives $\lVert x'\rVert_2^2=\lVert x\rVert_2^2+2h(y')^TKx+h^2\lVert K^Ty'\rVert_2^2$, $\lVert y'\rVert_2^2=\lVert y\rVert_2^2-2hy^TKx+h^2\lVert Kx\rVert_2^2$, and $-h(y')^TKx'=-h(y')^TKx-h^2\lVert K^Ty'\rVert_2^2$.

Suppose $h\lVert K\rVert_2>2$. By the zero-domain clause of [F3], the domain is nonzero; [F2]–[F4] then give unit right and left singular vectors $v,u$ for $\sigma=\lVert K\rVert_2$, with $Kv=\sigma u$ and $K^Tu=\sigma v$. The recurrence in step 2.1 preserves the two-dimensional coefficient subspace $x=av$, $y=bu$ and sends $(a,b)^T$ by $T_\sigma:=\begin{pmatrix}1-h^2\sigma^2&h\sigma\\-h\sigma&1\end{pmatrix}$. Its trace is $2-h^2\sigma^2<-2$ and determinant is $1$. Its characteristic polynomial has two distinct real negative reciprocal roots, one with modulus greater than $1$. An eigenvector for that root is an expanding singular mode.

Adding the identities in step 3.1 cancels the $\lVert K^Ty'\rVert_2^2$ terms; substituting $y'=y-hKx$ in the remainder gives $\lVert x'\rVert_2^2+\lVert y'\rVert_2^2-h(y')^TKx'=\lVert x\rVert_2^2+\lVert y\rVert_2^2-hy^TKx$. Therefore $E_h(x',y')=E_h(x,y)$ at each update.

By [F5] and [F3]–[F4], $|y^TKx|\le\lVert y\rVert_2\lVert Kx\rVert_2\le\lVert K\rVert_2\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$. Since $2\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2\le\lVert x\rVert_2^2+\lVert y\rVert_2^2$, the cross term in $E_h$ has absolute value at most $\tfrac12h\lVert K\rVert_2(\lVert x\rVert_2^2+\lVert y\rVert_2^2)$. Substitution gives both displayed energy bounds, whose lower coefficient is strictly positive when $h\lVert K\rVert_2<2$.

For every update, [F7] and [F6] give $Db_{n+1/2}=Db_{n-1/2}-hDCe_n=Db_{n-1/2}$, so induction preserves $Db$. The loop in [F7] has exactly the finite index set $0,\ldots,N-1$; each exact mass solve is unique by [F6] and step 1.1. It therefore terminates after $N$ updates, including the case $N=0$.

citations.quote:
Let $n_e,n_b,n_c,n_g$ be nonnegative integers. For dimension zero, $\mathbb R^0$ has its single empty vector and its unique square matrix acts as the identity on that space. Choose real matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$ and $M_b\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_b}$ that are symmetric positive definite, meaning $M_e^T=M_e$, $M_b^T=M_b$, $x^TM_ex>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and $y^TM_by>0$ for every nonzero $y\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$; these positivity conditions are vacuous on $\mathbb R^0$. Choose $C\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_e}$, a symmetric positive semidefinite $S\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$, meaning $S^T=S$ and $x^TSx\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and matrices $D\in\mathbb R^{n_c\times n_b}$ and $G\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_g}$ satisfying $DC=0$ and $CG=0$. These are finite real matrix data; no mesh or continuum field is assumed.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $j:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ be continuous, and let candidate states $e:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ and $b:I\to\mathbb R^{n_b}$ be of class $C^1$. The **finite compatible matrix system** is

$$M_e\dot e(t)=C^TM_bb(t)-Se(t)-j(t),\qquad \dot b(t)=-Ce(t)\quad(t\in I).$$

Its quadratic **energy** is $W(e,b):=\tfrac12(e^TM_ee+b^TM_bb)$. Its magnetic constraint is the vector $Db\in\mathbb R^{n_c}$. For the chosen $G$, its weak-divergence coordinate is $q:=-G^TM_ee\in\mathbb R^{n_g}$. The term “weak-divergence” names this finite-dimensional quantity only. If the columns of $G$ form a basis of $\ker C:=\{v\in\mathbb R^{n_e}:Cv=0\}$, then $q=0$ exactly when $M_ee\in\operatorname{im}C^T:=\{C^Tu:u\in\mathbb R^{n_b}\}$.

derivations.claim: The data satisfy the defining matrix assumptions: $M_e,M_b$ are positive definite, $S$ is positive semidefinite, and $DC=CG=0$. With $j=0$, [F1] reduces to $\dot e=b$ and $\dot b=-e$.
The forward Euler rule in the refuted statement therefore gives $e_1=e_0+h b_0$ and $b_1=b_0-h e_0$.

Expanding gives $W(e_1,b_1)=\tfrac12((e_0+h b_0)^2+(b_0-h e_0)^2)=(1+h^2)\tfrac12(e_0^2+b_0^2)=(1+h^2)W(e_0,b_0)$. Because $h>0$ and the initial pair is nonzero, $W(e_0,b_0)>0$ and $1+h^2>1$, so the step strictly increases energy. This refutes the universal preservation claim.

citations.quote:
Inputs are real matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$ and $M_b\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_b}$ that are symmetric positive definite, $C\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_e}$, and compatible matrices $D,G$ satisfying $DC=CG=0$, with $S=0$ and $j\equiv0$ in the finite compatible matrix system. All dimensions are nonnegative integers as in that system. Also input a real step size $h>0$, an integer horizon $N\ge0$, and initial vectors $e_0\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$ and $b_{-1/2}\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$. The matrix $M_e$ is positive definite, so each mass equation below has a unique exact solution, including the unique empty solve when $n_e=0$. For each integer $n=0,1,\ldots,N-1$, first set

$$b_{n+1/2}:=b_{n-1/2}-hCe_n,$$

then solve uniquely for $v_n\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$ in

$$M_ev_n=C^TM_bb_{n+1/2}$$

and set $e_{n+1}:=e_n+h v_n$. Output the electric vectors $e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ and magnetic vectors $b_{-1/2},b_{1/2},\ldots,b_{N-1/2}$. When $N=0$, the loop makes no updates and the output consists only of the two initial vectors. Every mass solve is exact; no inexact-solve error model is part of this procedure.

For the matrices and algorithm of the finite compatible matrix system, set $K:=M_b^{1/2}CM_e^{-1/2}:\mathbb R^{n_e}\to\mathbb R^{n_b}$. If $n_e=0$, define $\lVert K\rVert_2:=0$; if $n_e>0$, define $\lVert K\rVert_2:=\max_{\lVert x\rVert_2=1}\lVert Kx\rVert_2$, where $\lVert x\rVert_2:=(x^Tx)^{1/2}$. For a zero-dimensional symmetric positive-definite matrix, define its square root and inverse square root to be its unique $0\times0$ matrix. For a positive-dimensional real symmetric positive-definite matrix $M$, define $M^{1/2}$ by applying the positive scalar square root to its eigenvalues in an orthonormal eigenbasis, and define $M^{-1/2}:=(M^{1/2})^{-1}$. Call $h\lVert K\rVert_2<2$ the strict CFL condition for this finite matrix system. With $x_n:=M_e^{1/2}e_n$ and $y_{n-1/2}:=M_b^{1/2}b_{n-1/2}$, define

$$E_h(x_n,y_{n-1/2}):=\tfrac12\bigl(\lVert x_n\rVert_2^2+\lVert y_{n-1/2}\rVert_2^2-hy_{n-1/2}^TKx_n\bigr).$$

For every $N\ge0$, the algorithm terminates after $N$ updates. If $h\lVert K\rVert_2<2$, then each step preserves $E_h$, and

$$\frac{1-h\lVert K\rVert_2/2}{2}\bigl(\lVert x_n\rVert_2^2+\lVert y_{n-1/2}\rVert_2^2\bigr)\le E_h(x_n,y_{n-1/2})\le\frac{1+h\lVert K\rVert_2/2}{2}\bigl(\lVert x_n\rVert_2^2+\lVert y_{n-1/2}\rVert_2^2\bigr).$$

Consequently this modified energy is positive definite under the strict CFL condition. The constraint $Db_{n-1/2}$ is preserved. If $h\lVert K\rVert_2>2$, an expanding singular mode exists. Equality at $h\lVert K\rVert_2=2$ is excluded from both assertions; no stability claim is made there.

derivations.claim: These one-dimensional data satisfy the matrix assumptions of the algorithm. Their positive mass roots equal $1$, so [F2] gives $K=[1]$ and $h\lVert K\rVert_2=2$, exactly the endpoint in the refuted extension.

Write $z_n:=(e_n,b_{n-1/2})^T$. By [F1], $z_{n+1}=Az_n$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}-3&2\\-2&1\end{pmatrix}$. Set $J:=A+I=\begin{pmatrix}-2&2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$. Direct multiplication gives $J\ne0$ and $J^2=0$, so $A=-(I-J)$ and the binomial formula yields $A^n=(-1)^n(I-nJ)$ for every integer $n\ge0$.

For the nonzero initial state $z_0=(1,0)^T$, one has $Jz_0=(-2,-2)^T\ne0$. The reverse triangle inequality therefore gives $\lVert z_n\rVert_2=\lVert z_0-nJz_0\rVert_2\ge n\lVert Jz_0\rVert_2-\lVert z_0\rVert_2=2\sqrt2\,n-1$. These outputs occur in the algorithm for each finite horizon $N\ge n$ and their norm ratio to $\lVert z_0\rVert_2$ is unbounded as $n$ grows. No constant $C$ independent of $N$ can satisfy the refuted estimate.
